C1.justification: The central novelty and effectiveness claims remain. The introduction updates its highlighted relative gains from approximately 7% on GSM8K and 8% on LogiQA to 18% and 13%, respectively, using the added 70B-teacher results rather than changed results for the original setting.

C2.justification: v2 extends its interpretations to robustness across model scales, backbones and ranking choices, and makes the fine-grained-supervision explanation more assertive. It also substantially qualifies the efficiency discussion: ranking incurs approximately 2.3 times the training FLOPs while adding no inference overhead, and Appendix A.1 explicitly identifies training overhead as a limitation.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the GPTQ teacher checkpoint, QLoRA usage and DeepSpeed FLOPs Profiler for new experiments, while retaining the original hardware and main training hyperparameters. Conversely, the eight explicit GSM8K demonstrations in v1 Table 5 become a placeholder in v2 Table 7, reducing prompt disclosure.

E1.justification: v2 adds ASDiv, SVAMP and AQUA-RAT to examine mathematical reasoning across difficulty levels (Table 2). This extends coverage within an existing domain; CrossFit training and the five original target benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Vanilla, FT, C-Pretrain and Output-Align remain the comparison methods. The additional comparisons reuse these methods with different model configurations, training data or computational budgets. Newly cited alignment approaches such as IPO and KTO are not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds a quantized 70B teacher, a 13B student trained with QLoRA, and Phi-family configurations. It also introduces roughly FLOP-matched controls, intermediate-checkpoint comparisons and preference-consistency evaluation using 500 MMLU examples with five subsets each. The original benchmark settings and default training budget are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained subset-count, demonstration-count and source-task analyses, v2 adds direct preference-consistency measurements and controls testing whether additional computation or training data explain the gains. Section 5.2 and Appendix A.4–A.9 also investigate ranking formulations, subset sampling, KL scope, training progress, loss weights and contrastive-pair selection.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. v2's statements about no significant performance difference do not specify a statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: The original results in v1 Table 2 are preserved in v2 Table 1. Added results include 7B-student averages of 31.7 for BiAlign versus 30.0 for Output-Align with the new 70B teacher, and 39.6 versus 38.3 for a 13B student. Phi-family, additional mathematics, preference-consistency and extensive sensitivity/control results substantially expand the reported evidence.

M1.justification: The default BiAlign procedure, Equations 1–3 and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. v2 introduces a tested alternative ranking objective based on teacher–student probability-score gaps (Equation 4), constituting a limited methodological variant rather than a replacement of the core method.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes student/teacher terminology, revises author and front matter, and clarifies portions of the alignment discussion. Target-task descriptions move from Section 4.1 to Appendix A.3. The six-section main narrative and much of the existing prose remain, so editorial restructuring is limited.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. v1's introductory ICL example figure is removed, existing diagrams are resized and relabeled, and the main results table gains teacher-grouped blocks and shading. v2 adds numerous results tables and a preference-consistency plot, relocates the dataset table and substantially shortens the GSM8K example display.

R1.justification: v2 adds IPO and KTO to the alignment review and references supporting QLoRA, Phi, the quantized teacher and additional mathematics benchmarks. The main positioning against output-only distillation and the claimed novelty of input preference alignment remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds the mathematically distinct ranking-loss definition in Equation 4. The original loss equations, preference definitions and uniform-prior Bayesian argument are retained; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluates one student–teacher pair without directly measuring preference agreement or controlling for the ranking loss's additional computation. v2's broader model tests, preference-consistency analysis and roughly FLOP-matched controls substantially strengthen the central empirical argument (Section 5). Appendix diagnostics and the explicit overhead limitation further improve assessment of the method. Uncertainty remains unreported and prompt disclosure is reduced, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in experimental support and computational transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BiAlign, with readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting comparison. Visual inspection confirms that v1's appendix contains only a heading, whereas v2 contains Appendix A.1–A.10; this is a document difference, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: Sections 5.1–5.2 and Appendix A.4–A.9 retain original evaluations and report additional model comparisons, computational controls and sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original five-task evaluations, controlled analyses of demonstration and subset counts, and a generated-output comparison (Tables 2–5 and Figure 5).

C1.justification: The central contribution of jointly optimizing quantization and LoRA while producing quantized weights remains. v4 changes the potential inference-efficiency benefit into an achieved speed claim and strengthens v3's qualified superiority 'in most cases' into consistent-superiority language across a broader comparison. QAT-LoRA is also framed more explicitly as a baseline.

C2.justification: v3 says QAT-LoRA need not save weight gradients; v4 says it retains them and attributes L4Q's memory advantage to local computation and immediate disposal (Sections 3.1–3.2). v4 adds substantive outlier/clipping and rank-efficiency explanations and acknowledges higher training memory than PTQ-based PEFT. It removes v3's explicit weight-only limitation and activation/KV-cache future-work discussion.

D1.justification: Beyond v3's optimizer, hyperparameter, Lit-GPT, and GPU information, v4 specifies bfloat16 training, Hugging Face Transformers, gradient handling, measured training hours, and EXLLaMA2/GEMM inference kernels with layer exclusions and timing details. Its new reproducibility statement claims supplementary code and setup materials, but those materials and a usable source-code link are not present in the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: Both use Alpaca fine-tuning, the same seven Commonsense QA tasks, and MMLU. v4's Openbook QA wording does not establish added coverage: v3 already reports OBQA in its tables. Additional LLaMA-2 MMLU results extend model configurations within the existing tasks.

E2.justification: v4 adds GPTQ, OmniQuant, and uniformly quantized LoftQ* to the accuracy comparisons, adds QA-LoRA comparisons for LLaMA-2, and extends QAT-LoRA beyond v3's limited Figure 3 comparisons. Table 1 also expands the memory comparison from QAT/QAT-LoRA to include LoRA, QLoRA, LoftQ, QA-LoRA, and L4Q.

E3.justification: The stated training sequence length changes from 1304 to 2048, retaining the 128-token L4Q 33B exception. Several learning rates change, including L4Q's LLaMA-1 33B and LLaMA-2 rates from 1e-4 to 2e-4. New protocols include initialization/rank controls and inference timing over 2000 data points, 512 tokens, and batch sizes 1–64. These documented changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds comparisons of four initialization schemes with initial/post-training quantization and clipping errors (Section 3.3 and Appendix B), plus a rank 1–128 sensitivity study on Commonsense QA and MMLU (Appendix D). Appendix G examines the throughput cost of an unmerged LoRA path across batch sizes. v3's warm-up analysis is retained as Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates. v4's weight-distribution standard deviations and quantization-error measurements are not uncertainty estimates for experimental outcomes.

E6.justification: All 38 earlier Commonsense QA table rows are retained unchanged, but MMLU and memory values change alongside substantial new results. For example, v3 Figure 3 reports L4Q/QAT-LoRA at 31.5/31.8 on 3-bit LLaMA-1 7B MMLU 5-shot; v4 Table 3 reports 31.8/31.5. L4Q's 33B 3-bit MMLU averages change from 49.4/50.8 to 50.5/53.1. Changed settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains. Initialization, rank, timing, throughput, and additional comparator results are newly reported.

M1.justification: v3 Algorithm 1 initializes scale as AbsMax(W0+alpha BA)/Qp. v4 replaces this with L4Qinit, using the maximum of the separately normalized negative and positive extrema (Equation 12). This refines initialization while retaining merged-weight quantization, learned scale/bias, LoRA updates, and warm-up. The expanded gradient-storage explanation does not establish a newly implemented update procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, method explanation, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Methods expands from two to four subsections, efficiency discussion is reorganized, the limitations section disappears, and a reproducibility statement is added. Appendices are reorganized and expanded, with author-year citations replacing numbered citations.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn from an adaptation-path diagram into an accuracy-versus-speedup comparison. v3's QAT-LoRA comparison chart gives way to tabulated comparisons, while v4 adds initialization and speedup plots. Detailed benchmark tables move to Appendix H and are expanded; new main-text summaries separate 4-bit and 3-bit results. Memory, ablation, and runtime tables substantially expand the displays.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations to OmniQuant, LLM.int8(), and nonuniform-to-uniform quantization, and develops the previously cited LoftQ into a substantive discussion of SVD-based initialization and its limitations. References associated with removed discussion, including Optimal Brain Compression and KV-cache work, disappear. The central positioning against PTQ-based PEFT remains.

T1.justification: v4 introduces the revised mathematical initialization definition in Equation 12 and explicit initialization rules in Appendix B. Appendix A retains the substantive STE, quantization-gradient, and LoRA-gradient derivations; most additional intermediate equations expand existing reasoning rather than supply new proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the paper's central efficiency case: v3 explicitly deferred speed measurement, whereas v4 provides measured throughput, L4Q-specific memory comparisons, and training times with documented kernels and procedures. Initialization and rank ablations also make important design choices more assessable. These gains outweigh the removed explicit limitations discussion and remaining overstatements: for example, Table 3 reports L4Q at 50.0 versus QLoRA* at 50.6 on LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot, qualifying the claimed consistent superiority.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same L4Q research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds initialization and rank experiments, broader baseline comparisons, training times, and inference-throughput measurements.

before.justification: v3 reports original Commonsense QA and MMLU accuracies, training-memory measurements, and a LoRA warm-up experiment.

results.title: L4Q: Parameter Efficient Quantization-Aware Fine-Tuning on Large Language Models

C1.justification: The contribution changes from a four-category assessment of 13 attacks to a six-category assessment of 17 attacks. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion foreground defense evaluation and the claim that attacks without initial jailbreak seeds are harder to defend against, substantially extending v1's attack-effectiveness and transferability claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting initial-seed patterns to transferability and defense susceptibility, and interprets temporal changes as possible model updates. It also explicitly acknowledges inability to assess harmful-response correctness and potential biases from generated questions and auxiliary LLMs. These materially qualify and extend v1's interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 Table 10 and Appendix A.5 add substantial implementation information, including auxiliary models, LAA template selection, COLD's suffix configuration, AdvPrompter training, MasterKey's GPT-4 rewriting, and defense configurations. Hardware details are retained in prose. Some specificity is lost: v1's explicit GCG batch size and named question-generation models are no longer stated.

E1.justification: The 160-question, 16-category evaluation coverage is retained. However, v2 adds substantially different test environments: systems protected by individual and combined external defenses, and changing commercial-model deployments over time (Sections 7.4 and 8).

E2.justification: DrAttack, LAA, COLD, and AdvPrompter join the evaluated attacks in both direct and transfer comparisons. Tables 2 and 5 expand from 13 to 17 direct methods and five to nine transfer methods, retaining the original comparators. Eight external defenses are also newly compared in Table 7.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama3-8B and Llama3.1-8B target configurations, biweekly longitudinal testing, and individual/combined defense evaluations using bypass rate alongside ASR. Table 10 also specifies AdvPrompter fine-tuning on the default AdvBench split for ten epochs. Its GCG limit changes from v1 Table 8's 50 to 500, resolving the conflict with v1's already-stated 500-step main-text setting; this does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial robustness analyses of attack persistence across model updates and resistance to eight defenses individually and jointly. Figure 6 and Table 7 address questions absent from v1. The existing transferability, runtime, and token-length analyses are retained and extended.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three repetitions and mean/standard-deviation reporting; this disclosure moves from v1 Section 5.4 to v2 Appendix A.2. The 640-response validation, three annotators, majority vote, and agreement statistic are retained. No new statistical estimation or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive attack/model, defense, and longitudinal results. The expanded comparison identifies LAA as strongest overall, with average direct ASR 0.85 across eight models (Table 2). Table 7 reports LAA falling to 0.00 under Prompt-Guard, while DrAttack retains 0.34 under all defenses combined. Most shared attack/model scores remain; changed averages over expanded comparator or model sets are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The work remains an assessment of existing methods, without an established procedural change to the shared attacks. The actual GPT-4 judging prompt is identical in v1 Figure 9 and v2 Figure 8. Reclassifying attacks and adding evaluated methods do not introduce a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, taxonomy discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The optimization-based category becomes three separate categories, token-length and runtime subsections exchange order, and substantial discussion moves into an appendix organized into six subsections. v1's ethical-considerations paragraph is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adds a taxonomy table, longitudinal plots, and a large defense-results table, while expanding and restructuring attack tables and heatmaps. v1's pooled direct/transfer heatmaps are removed, token plots are regrouped, and the question-generation prompt and response-misjudgment table move to the appendix. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning toward attack robustness and defense evaluation. It adds references for the four new attacks, perplexity defenses, Erase, Self-Reminder, and longitudinal robustness, alongside new model resources. The earlier coordinate-descent reference is removed; many existing references are simply renumbered.

T1.justification: The ASR definition is retained, and neither version presents theoretical proofs or theorems. v2 adds the standard bypass-rate formula for its defense evaluation, without new mathematical reasoning or formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: The longitudinal and defense evaluations address an important gap in v1: strong static attack results did not establish persistence under model updates or external safeguards. Table 7 materially qualifies the rankings, showing that LAA's high unprotected ASR collapses under Prompt-Guard while other attacks remain effective. Added implementation details and explicit response-quality limitations strengthen interpretation. These gains outweigh limited documentation problems, including the new mismatch between Section 5.3's B/C label descriptions and the unchanged appendix judge prompt.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 18 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations of further attacks and models, longitudinal measurements, and external defenses.

before.justification: v1 reports original direct and transfer attack experiments, runtime and token-count measurements, and human validation of its response judge.

results.title: JailbreakRadar: Comprehensive Assessment of Jailbreak Attacks Against LLMs

C1.justification: The central claim that description order affects graph reasoning remains. However, v4 drops the headline nonmonotonic graph-size finding and SGR scaling-benchmark contribution. It instead foregrounds task-dependent robustness, suitability of different orders, and GraphDO as a six-task benchmark.

C2.justification: v1's explanations emphasize model laziness, graph size and short-term memory. v4 develops attention/positional-encoding bias and local-versus-global reasoning explanations, interprets answer-overlap tests, and discusses hallucinated edges in response cases. It also explicitly acknowledges insufficient exploration of graph structures and the absence of rigorous theoretical explanations.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's brief settings and schematic prompts, v4 supplies extensive reproducibility information in Appendices A-C: prompt templates, personalization parameters, graph-generation and sampling instructions, graph/case counts, response parsing and GPT-based judging, NetworkX use, and four-A800 hardware. These are substantial additions to documentation; settings absent from v1 do not establish that its implementation differed.

E1.justification: Connectivity, cycle detection and shortest path remain, but v4 adds Hamilton path, directed topological sorting and node classification on CORA, Citeseer and Pubmed. GraphDO replaces the NLGraph/SGR evaluation framework. The addition of directed graphs and attributed citation graphs substantially broadens the represented tasks and domains.

E2.justification: The evaluated order set adds PR and PPR on retained tasks and removes second-shortest-path ordering. Prompt comparisons expand to include zero-shot CoT and CoT-BAG, while v1's TEXT-DAVINCI-003 reference comparison disappears. Shortest-path and longest-path orders are retained in v4's deeper exploration, rather than removed.

E3.justification: v1's difficulty-stratified NLGraph evaluation and SGR edge-count sweeps are replaced by GraphDO experiments using ER graphs with 5-15 nodes and connection probability 0.3. v4 adds citation-graph sampling protocols and Qwen2, Mistral and Vicuna configurations. The stated Llama decoding temperature changes from 0.7 to zero, and evaluation expands from three to five prompt conditions.

E4.justification: v4 removes the graph-size sweeps and associated model-laziness investigation. It adds cross-order variance analysis of task sensitivity and concrete successful and erroneous response cases in Appendix D. The existing shortest/longest-order experiment is revised into an explicit answer-overlap investigation using GraphDO and two prompting conditions.

E5.justification: v4 Appendix C newly reports three repetitions for the node-classification experiments; v1 provides no repeated-run counts. Neither version reports confidence intervals or run-to-run error bars. The variance in v4 Figure 4 measures sensitivity across description orders, rather than uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: The numerical evidence is substantially replaced and expanded. For example, v1 Table 1 reports NLGraph easy CoT shortest-path default/BFS accuracies of 42.22/55.00%, whereas v4 Table 1 reports GraphDO CoT random/BFS accuracies of 38.93/67.50%. These are different-setting results, not cross-version performance gains. v4 also adds Hamilton-path, topological-sort and citation-graph classification results, while removing the size-dependent curves.

M1.justification: v4 adds PageRank and task-specific Personalized PageRank procedures for constructing edge orders, beyond v1's traversal and path-based orders. Section 3.2 also changes the reported BFS/DFS edge-completion procedure from appending unvisited edges to traversing a dual graph. These change the input-construction procedure, while retaining the general approach of prompting an unchanged LLM.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the explanatory prose are rewritten. v4 condenses the preliminary discussion, creates a dedicated graph-description methodology section, organizes main findings around Q1-Q3, and separates deeper exploration. Dataset and implementation explanations are redistributed into new appendices, with additional limitations and ethics sections.

P2.justification: v4 redraws the introductory and framework diagrams, replaces the size-sweep displays with task/order/model panels, and adds a variance chart and heatmaps summarizing main results. Main tables are reorganized around prompt styles and dataset/sampling combinations. Appendix prompt-template and response-case tables provide additional displays.

R1.justification: v1 positions SGR as a continuous-scale refinement of NLGraph's discrete difficulty levels; v4 replaces that positioning with an order-focused GraphDO benchmark. The research context also expands to GraphText, GITA, pseudo-code prompting and primacy effects, with additional model, prompting and dataset literature. This goes beyond bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: v4 adds PR/PPR recurrences and formal task-specific personalization distributions in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2, alongside definitions of the additional graph problems. This expands the mathematical specification beyond v1's order-optimization and sparsity formulations, but adds no theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially improves the support and auditability of the central ordering claim. Tables 1-2 expose task-dependent behavior across structural and citation-graph problems, while Appendices A-C address major documentation gaps in v1 through explicit prompts, sampling, counts and response judging. The size-scaling investigation is lost, and solution-informed PPR plus the unjustified BFS explanation for weighted shortest paths limit mechanistic conclusions. Nevertheless, the clearer experimental comparisons and substantially fuller implementation record provide a clear net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs study how graph-description order affects LLM graph reasoning, despite the changed title and substantially revised experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison throughout. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v4 includes readable Appendices A-D.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments on GraphDO and sampled citation graphs in Tables 1-2, additional ordering and model experiments in Figures 6-7, and response examples in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-2 experiments on NLGraph and SGR in Table 1 and Figures 4-6. Table 2 separately identifies TEXT-DAVINCI-003 results borrowed from prior work.

results.title: Can Graph Descriptive Order Affect Solving Graph Problems with LLMs?

C1.justification: v3 presents the codec/language-model training-data gap and use of the largest training dataset as central motivations and contributions. v4 removes that gap from the abstract and introduction and replaces the data-scale/hyperparameter contribution with emphasis on decoder architecture and discrimination. The central MCRVQ, four-codebook reconstruction and downstream usefulness claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 attributes reconstruction advantages partly to greater training-data volume. v4's Appendix A instead reports little reconstruction dependence on dataset size, including the internal Chinese data, and suggests that scale may matter more for multilingual generalization. New component analyses refine architectural explanations, while Section 7 explicitly limits demonstrated applicability to speech training and downstream speech models.

D1.justification: Appendix I and Figure 2 add decoder layer ordering, convolution kernels, strides, padding, normalization and attention wiring. Most existing optimizer, hardware and training information is relocated to Appendix C. Reported release status becomes less clear: v3 says code, pretrained models and demos are already open, while v4 promises future code/model release despite its abstract saying code is available.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same training-data mixture, LibriTTS clean/noisy reconstruction, LJSpeech generalization and LibriSpeech zero-shot TTS coverage. v4's additional experiments vary training subsets, components and quantizer counts within this coverage. Appendix E relocates existing evaluation scenarios.

E2.justification: DAC is added at 3 and 6 kbps to the LibriTTS Test-Clean and Test-Other comparisons, while Lyra-v2 is removed from those comparisons (v3 Table 1; v4 Tables 1 and 6). Lyra-v2 remains in LJSpeech, whose comparator membership is unchanged. The downstream TTS comparator set is also retained.

E3.justification: v4 substantially expands the experimental controls: training on 585-hour LibriTTS, excluding the 20,000-hour internal dataset, removing decoder/discriminator components, and comparing four versus eight quantizers in MobileSpeech. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, primary training budgets and listening-study procedures are retained. An actual crop-duration change is unresolved: Section 3.2 says three seconds, whereas Appendix C retains v3's one-second setting.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's MCRVQ ablations and pretrained Encodec/Vocos comparisons, v4 adds direct Language-Codec decoder replacement and attention-removal tests, discriminator removal, training-data-volume controls and downstream quantizer-count analysis (Appendices A, F-H). These investigate component contributions, dependence on training data and the quality tradeoff from fewer codebooks.

E5.justification: Both versions report MOS values with ± quantities and specify 50 subjective-evaluation samples with at least ten listeners per sample. v4 adds no seed counts, repeated-run information, significance tests or explanation of uncertainty estimation. Table 10 extends the existing MOS reporting practice.

E6.justification: Language-Codec results are extensively revised across all three reconstruction corpora, downstream TTS and MCRVQ ablations. For example, four-channel LibriTTS Test-Clean UTMOS changes from 3.6191 to 3.7875, and VALL-E/Language-Codec WER and SPK change from 4.1/0.6806 to 3.8/0.6995. DAC results and new ablation/configuration results are added. These are results for a revised model, not demonstrated gains under an unchanged method and training configuration.

M1.justification: v4 adds an attention module containing convolutional residual blocks and self-attention before the decoder's ConvNeXt blocks, substantially extending the convolutional decoder described in v3 (Section 3.2 and Appendix I). The encoder, MCRVQ procedure, Fourier reconstruction and loss equations remain unchanged. The discriminator types emphasized in v4 were already described in v3.

P1.justification: v4 reworks the motivation, contributions and related-work narrative, changes the title and author information, and reorganizes substantial existing material into appendices. Baselines, training settings, human evaluation and noisy/out-of-domain evaluations move out of the main text, while conclusions, acknowledgments and limitations receive separate sections.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is extensively redrawn, and Figure 2 adds four decoder-component panels. The original combined LibriTTS table is split between main-text Table 1 and appendix Table 6; LJSpeech moves to Table 7. Four new analysis tables are added, alongside substantial changes to typography, spacing, captions and document layout.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion shifts from separate codec and zero-shot TTS surveys toward codec architectures and the reconstruction/generation gap. v4 adds HILCodec, APCodec and SemantiCodec discussion, cites WavTokenizer and expands discussion of the already-cited DAC work. It removes the TTS survey containing VALL-E X, NaturalSpeech2, Mega-TTS and Make-a-Voice.

T1.justification: The mathematical content of Equations 1-13, covering signal representation, MCRVQ and training losses, is retained. The new decoder diagram uses standard attention notation but adds no substantive theoretical development, revised derivation, formal assumption or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central design choices. Table 5 directly tests the training-scale explanation emphasized in v3; Tables 8-9 isolate discriminator and decoder contributions; Table 10 tests four-codebook downstream generation. These address important attribution and practical-validation gaps, while decoder details and explicit speech-only limitations improve assessability. Conflicting crop durations and less clear release statements weaken reproducibility, but do not outweigh the added diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Language-Codec and its MCRVQ mechanism. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. All nine pages of v3 and fourteen pages of v4 were inspected, including v4's Appendices A-I; v3 has no appendix.

after.justification: v4 reports original reconstruction and speech synthesis results, plus training-data, decoder, discriminator and quantizer-count experiments in Tables 1-10.

before.justification: v3 reports original codec reconstruction, zero-shot speech synthesis, human evaluation and MCRVQ ablation results in Tables 1-5.

results.title: Language-Codec: Bridging Discrete Codec Representations and Speech Language Models

C1.justification: The central claim of improving alignment without additional training remains. However, v3 makes small parameter changes without new knowledge injection, and first-order improvement of an implicit objective, central claims in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Stated applicability expands from 7B–70B to 1.8B–70B and includes MT-Bench. The headline off-the-shelf LC gain changes from 6.8 percentage points in v1's prose to 4.5 in v3, matching the retained Tulu-2-70B comparison.

C2.justification: v3 interprets excessive extrapolation and overtraining failures through breakdown of the first-order approximation and develops optimizer-dependent explanations. It adds a substantive alignment-tax limitation, a tradeoff between training savings and downstream degradation, and a possible input-template confound (§6). v1's checkpoint-availability limitation and explanation of scalability through stronger SFT models are no longer developed.

D1.justification: v3 documents detailed search traces, intervals, timing, and inference hardware in Appendix B, expands checkpoint identifiers in Appendix C, and specifies lm-evaluation-harness 0.4.4. Reported training hardware changes from four to eight A100 GPUs. Conversely, v1's explicit DPO beta of 0.01, gradient accumulation, ZeRO-3, checkpointing, warmup and scheduling details, and exact GPT-4 judge snapshot are omitted.

E1.justification: UltraFeedback and AlpacaEval 2.0 remain. v3 adds MT-Bench's multi-turn evaluation and six downstream tasks: ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, and GSM8K (§6 and Appendix D). These substantially broaden evaluation beyond the original preference-alignment benchmarks.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained DPO/RLHF comparisons, v3 Table 6 evaluates RRHF, SLiC-HF, IPO, CPO, KTO, R-DPO, and SimPO models against their ExPO counterparts. Table 5 also adds Snorkel and LLaMA-3 iterative-DPO models and three InternLM2 models. These are actual reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v3 adds a second reward-model evaluator for interpolation, GPT-4 scoring from 1 to 10 for MT-Bench, downstream evaluations, and sorted-data and optimizer controls. Model configurations expand to include 1.8B, 8B, and 20B models. Rephrasing data fractions as training-step fractions is equivalent under the retained one-epoch recipe. Table 4's '2e-6 (×3)' learning-rate entry is internally inconsistent, leaving that particular setting ambiguous.

E4.justification: v3 adds parameter-change measurements, reward-distribution analysis, deliberate length-bias injection, AdaGrad/RMSprop ablations, and alignment-tax analysis (§§1, 3 and 6; Appendix D). The existing epoch and learning-rate study is retained in condensed form. v1's quantitative tests of separately trained checkpoint pairs and its 5%-data sensitivity curve disappear, while v3 adds the Storm-7B collapse case.

E5.justification: v3 §3.1 newly specifies generation random seed 42; v1 does not state a sampling seed. No explicit increase in repeated runs or new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Many retained scores are identical, including the 20%-trained ExPO model's 21.3% AlpacaEval LC win rate. v3 adds the 40% condition's AlpacaEval results, MT-Bench scores, other-algorithm results, and downstream findings. For example, Table 5 reports LLaMA-3 iterative DPO improving from 8.08 to 8.45 on MT-Bench. Some baseline scores change: Zephyr-alpha's raw win rate is 8.4% in v1 versus 6.7% in v3. Since v1 explicitly selected the higher of reproduced and leaderboard scores, this is a revised comparison, not an established same-setting regression. The off-the-shelf reward-score column is removed.

M1.justification: v1 Equation 2 and v3 Equation 6 implement the same update: add alpha times the difference between the aligned and initial SFT checkpoints. Both select alpha using reward scores on the UltraFeedback development set. The new derivation and applications to additional alignment algorithms do not change ExPO's procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodology, and conclusion are extensively rewritten.
